title: Tea for the Other Side
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 41 · The Seventh Ring arc
content:
Iroh had two rules about visitors.

The first was that nobody left the Jasmine Dragon thirsty if he could help it.

The second was that nobody was required to explain why they had come.

He broke the first rule himself on the morning the deliveries went wrong.

A crate of silver spoons appeared on the shop's back step. Each spoon had a tiny hammer stamped beneath its handle, the mark of Brasswatch Yard. The jasmine tea Iroh had ordered from the vale was nowhere to be found.

He stood over the spoons with the expression of a man examining an army that had arrived at the wrong gate.

“Well,” he said, “they are remarkably poor at steeping.”

I bent to inspect the crate. “Maybe you asked for strong tea.”

“I see you have joined the enemy.”

I picked up a spoon. It was heavy, handmade, and slightly crooked. Someone had put effort into it. Whoever had packed the crate expected the tools to reach people who needed them. Now they had to be carried back.

“Can we send them through the Jasmine Door?”

“Of course.”

“Without anyone knowing where they were meant to go?”

Iroh took the spoon from me and set it down carefully.

“Ah. A question about intention and consequence.”

“A question about labels.”

“Those are frequently related.”

We closed the shop for one hour, hung a note on the door, and went to Lanternwell Square. Iroh carried the crate himself until I reminded him the handles were cutting into his palms. He conceded the point with a sigh designed to make me feel like a tyrant.

At the square, Greg was arguing with the notice board.

“It's not that I don't want to make a list,” he said. “I just think the list needs to explain what a list is for.”

Toph leaned against the stone wall, arms folded. “That's a fancy way to say you didn't write one.”

“I wrote three! Then I lost the second one.”

“Proving my point.”

Iroh presented the crate as if arriving at a royal banquet.

“Silver spoons,” he announced. “Very interesting. Entirely incapable of becoming tea.”

Toph took one, ran a thumb across the maker's mark, and frowned.

“Not spoons,” she said. “Setting tools. Who told you they were spoons?”

I lifted both hands. “I said silver. I made no claims about their social aspirations.”

Greg laughed. Toph did not.

“They're from the repair yard. And that bend's on purpose.”

Iroh looked pleased. “Then I have learned something new. A very good morning.”

Neri joined us beneath the lanterns and explained the troubled bell. We listened. Iroh asked questions about people who had carried medicine. I asked about the supplies that might spoil while they waited to be claimed. Greg offered to help with an inventory; Toph volunteered to test every wheel in the mechanism, provided nobody described the work as ‘feeling things out.’

For a little while it felt easy.

Then a young courier from Riverstone Terrace arrived carrying a sealed jar of medicine from Moonroot Archive. He had been told to deliver it to the clinic. Instead the jar had followed him into the Jasmine Steps tea stall.

Katara was still waiting.

The courier's hands shook as he told us.

Iroh went very quiet.

There were many people who admired his calm. I knew what it cost him. Calm was a skill he had learned through years when the wrong order could send a regiment to its death. A missing medicine jar was not a war. It was still somebody else's fear.

“Show me the label,” he said.

The courier handed it over. Iroh checked the name, the destination, and the seal without touching the contents. Then he gave the jar back.

“You will take this through the correct door,” he said. “I will walk with you. Jasper, would you tell Neri where we have gone?”

I stared at him. “You don't need an escort.”

“No,” he agreed. “He does.”

The courier swallowed hard.

Iroh did not pat his shoulder or tell him he had nothing to be ashamed of. He simply walked beside him at the speed of someone carrying something precious.

I stayed behind to write the entry in Neri's book.

Toph watched me.

“You're worried.”

“Remarkably sharp.”

“Don't be an idiot. I'm blind, not oblivious.”

I smiled in spite of myself.

She reached for another of the tools and turned it between her fingers. “You can love somebody and still hate seeing them walk toward danger.”

“Doesn't seem very fair.”

“Lots of things aren't.”

Greg joined us with a pencil tucked behind one ear.

“Can I ask something?” he said.

“You already have.”

“I mean about the doors. If a crate goes through because somebody carries it, but the door doesn't recognize who should get it, is the problem the door or the people?”

We considered that.

“Both,” I said. “Maybe neither. The problem is assuming a choice has been made just because a thing moved.”

Toph tapped the tool on the wall.

“Then give everybody a chance to say where their stuff belongs.”

She said it like it was obvious.

I had learned not to mistake obvious for easy.

When Iroh returned, he carried an empty basket and looked exhausted in a way he would never admit. The medicine had reached Katara. The courier had received tea and directions home. Nobody had been hurt.

I met him beside the well.

“You didn't have to do all that.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He looked toward the Riverstone Door.

“Because he was afraid,” Iroh said. “And because once, I was the sort of man who would have sent a young person ahead while I waited in safety.”

I took his hand. He let me.

“I love the man who walked with him,” I said.

A faint smile touched his mouth. “He is fortunate.”

“He is going to have to sit down and drink water.”

“That sounds less romantic.”

“I'm a complicated person.”

Iroh bent close. His kiss tasted faintly of jasmine and the warm salt of a day spent carrying other people's worry. When he drew back, his face held that rare, unguarded happiness I never wanted to turn into a lesson.

“May I ask you to stay for supper?” he said.

“You may.”

“Even if there are no silver spoons?”

“Especially then.”

Back at the Jasmine Dragon, he set out two cups and one additional place for the courier if he returned.

The order of tea had finally arrived.

I could have called it a small victory. Instead I wrote the delivery down, marked who had carried it, and took a second look at the handwriting on the crate.

Someone had written the wrong destination before the package ever reached the door.

Iroh saw my face.

“What is it?”

“I think,” I said, “we need to find out who has been changing the labels.”

He did not smile.

He reached for the ledger.
